US History – Unit Overview

The Vietnam War

A war that divided a nation, shattered a generation, and changed what America thought it was capable of.
1 9 5 5  –  1 9 7 5
Chapter 1
What Was the Vietnam War?
Civil War, Proxy War, Cold War
A South Vietnamese soldier questions a suspected Viet Cong fighter

Before there was a Vietnam War, there was a Vietnam. A country that had been fighting outsiders for centuries, French colonizers, Japanese occupiers, and hadn't stopped yet. By the time American soldiers arrived, the Vietnamese had already been at war for a generation.

The French controlled Southeast Asia from the 1800s until 1954, when Vietnamese nationalist forces called the Viet Minh handed them a devastating defeat at the Battle of Dien Bien Phu. It was over for France. But it wasn't over for Vietnam.

The Geneva Accords of 1954 ended French rule and divided the country at the 17th Parallel. North Vietnam went to the communist government of Ho Chi Minh. South Vietnam got an American-backed, anti-communist government. There were supposed to be elections in 1956 to reunify the country. Those elections never happened. The US made sure of it.

So what exactly was the Vietnam War? It was three things at once. It was a civil war between Vietnamese who wanted a unified communist country and those who didn't. It was a proxy war, with the US, Soviet Union, and China all backing opposite sides. And it was a Cold War showdown, a test of whether the United States would hold the line against communism in Southeast Asia. Those three layers made it almost impossible to fight, and almost impossible to win.

The elections that were supposed to reunify Vietnam never happened. The US made sure of it. And that decision, made quietly, thousands of miles away, lit a fuse that would burn for twenty years.
Ho Chi Minh
President, North Vietnam
Click to learn more
A revolutionary who spent decades fighting for Vietnamese independence, first against the French, then against the Americans. He had once appealed to Woodrow Wilson at Versailles for Vietnamese self-determination and been ignored. By the time of the war he was mostly a symbolic figure, but his name meant everything to the North.
John F. Kennedy
US President, 1961–1963
Click to learn more
Kennedy inherited a messy situation and made it bigger, quietly, without headlines. He sent military advisors and equipment to South Vietnam but was deeply uneasy about a full ground war. He said it was "their war to win or lose." Whether he would have escalated the way Johnson did is one of history's great unanswered questions. We'll never know.
Ngo Dinh Diem
President, South Vietnam
Click to learn more
America's chosen man in Saigon, and a disaster. Catholic in a country that was 80% Buddhist, he handed the best jobs to family members and persecuted anyone who opposed him. His brutal crackdown on Buddhist monks in 1963 shocked the world. By November of that year, his own generals overthrew him with a quiet nod from Washington. He was murdered in the back of an armored vehicle.
Chapter 2
Why Did the US Get Involved?
Domino Theory and US Credibility

Nobody decided to fight a war in Vietnam. It crept up on the United States, one small commitment at a time, until suddenly there were half a million American troops there and no good way out.

The logic went like this: the Domino Theory. If South Vietnam fell to communism, then Laos, Cambodia, Thailand, and the rest of Southeast Asia would follow. After watching China fall in 1949 and fighting to a stalemate in Korea, American presidents from Eisenhower to Johnson believed they simply could not afford to let another country go communist on their watch.

There was also the question of credibility. The United States had made promises to South Vietnam. Walking away would send a message to every American ally in the world: don't count on us. In the Cold War, that was a message no president wanted to send.

And so the commitment grew. Military advisors. Equipment. Money. Then, in August 1964, an incident in the Gulf of Tonkin gave President Johnson the opening he needed. US ships were reportedly attacked by North Vietnamese torpedo boats. Johnson went to Congress and got a blank check, the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, authorizing him to use military force however he saw fit. Later investigations revealed the second attack almost certainly never happened. But by then, the war had already been decided.

Lyndon B. Johnson
US President, 1963–1969
Click to learn more
The man who turned a slow bleed into a full-scale war. LBJ used the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution to pour troops into Vietnam while simultaneously building his Great Society programs at home. He genuinely believed he could win, until he couldn't. By 1968, unpopular and broken by the war, he announced he wouldn't run for reelection. Vietnam consumed his presidency.
Robert McNamara
Secretary of Defense
Click to learn more
The architect of American strategy in Vietnam, and one of its most tortured critics. McNamara pushed escalation with cold statistical logic: body counts, kill ratios, metrics that turned out to mean almost nothing. Years later he admitted he knew by 1967 the war was unwinnable but said nothing publicly. "We were wrong, terribly wrong," he wrote. Too late for 58,000 Americans.
Nguyễn Cao Kỳ
Vice President, South Vietnam
Click to learn more
The flashy Air Force general who became South Vietnam's Vice President. Known for his purple scarves and fighter pilot swagger, Ky represented everything unstable about the South Vietnamese government, a revolving door of generals and coups that never earned the trust of its own people. He fled to the United States in 1975 as Saigon fell.
Chapter 3
How Was Vietnam Different From Other Wars?
Kill Ratio, Body Count, Search and Destroy
US troops on patrol, Vietnam, 1966

In World War II, you knew where the front line was. You took territory, held it, pushed forward. Vietnam was nothing like that.

The US military had more firepower, more technology, and more money than any army in history. And it was fighting an enemy that refused to stand still and fight. The Viet Cong were guerrilla fighters. They struck at night, blended into villages, planted booby traps, and melted back into the jungle. A soldier could go an entire tour without seeing the enemy face to face. But he could step on a landmine any time he left base.

General Westmoreland's strategy was search and destroy. Find the enemy, kill them, count the bodies. Progress was measured in body counts. The more enemy dead, the better we were supposedly doing. But this logic had a fatal flaw: you couldn't body-count your way to victory in a war where the other side was willing to keep dying indefinitely, where North Vietnam could replace every soldier it lost, and where the people of South Vietnam weren't always sure they were on your side.

Then came Tet. On January 31, 1968, the Vietnamese New Year, the Viet Cong and North Vietnamese launched simultaneous surprise attacks on more than 100 cities across South Vietnam. They hit the US Embassy in Saigon. They seized the ancient city of Hue. Americans watching the news couldn't believe what they were seeing. The military had been telling them for years that we were winning. This didn't look like winning. Tet didn't end the war, but it shattered the public's trust. And that trust never came back.

Walter Cronkite, the most trusted man in America, looked into the camera after Tet and told the country the war was a stalemate. When LBJ heard what Cronkite said, he turned off the TV and told an aide: "If I've lost Cronkite, I've lost Middle America."
Gen. Westmoreland
US Commander, Vietnam
Click to learn more
The face of American military confidence in Vietnam, and its most famous blind spot. Westmoreland consistently told the public and Congress that the war was being won, that there was "light at the end of the tunnel." Then Tet happened. His strategy of attrition, grinding down the enemy through sheer firepower, never accounted for an opponent willing to suffer almost any losses to win.
Võ Nguyên Giáp
General, North Vietnam
Click to learn more
The military genius on the other side. Giap had already beaten the French at Dien Bien Phu, moving thousands of artillery pieces through jungle by hand. Against the Americans, his strategy was simpler: don't lose. Make the war so long and so costly that the American public would demand it end. He was right. He outlasted them all.
Chapter 4
How Did Vietnam Divide America?
The War Comes Home
Moratorium Day, October 15, 1969

Vietnam Moratorium, October 15, 1969. An estimated 2 million Americans participated in what became the largest single-day antiwar demonstration in US history. Rallies, teach-ins, and marches took place in hundreds of cities and towns. It wasn't organized by radicals or fringe groups. It was teachers, clergy, business owners, and suburban families who had simply had enough. Nixon called them "an effete corps of impudent snobs" and claimed the protests had no effect on his policy. But his own aides later admitted the scale of Moratorium Day forced the White House to pull back plans to escalate the bombing of North Vietnam.

The war didn't just divide America from Vietnam. It divided America from itself.

By 1967, the antiwar movement had grown from a fringe campus protest into something that filled the streets of every major American city. Hawks believed the US had to hold the line against communism, whatever the cost. Doves wanted out, and they wanted out now. The argument wasn't just about strategy. It was about what kind of country America was.

The draft made the fault lines visible. College students could get deferments. Working-class kids and Black Americans couldn't. A disproportionate number of those dying in Vietnam were the ones who had the fewest choices at home. Martin Luther King Jr. called it out directly in his 1967 "Beyond Vietnam" speech: America was sending Black men to die for freedoms in Southeast Asia they didn't have in Southwest Georgia.

In May 1970, Nixon secretly expanded the war into Cambodia. When the news broke, campuses exploded. At Kent State University in Ohio, National Guard troops opened fire on unarmed student protesters, killing four and wounding nine. Two million Americans joined a national day of protest. 400,000 marched in Washington, the largest antiwar demonstration in US history.

Then came the Pentagon Papers. In 1971, researcher Daniel Ellsberg leaked a classified study showing the Johnson administration had systematically lied to the American people about the war. The New York Times published them. Nixon tried to stop the presses. The Supreme Court said no. Americans learned their government had been deceiving them for years. The damage to public trust was permanent.

Vietnamese civilians flee fighting in the Mekong Delta
Vietnam Veterans Against the War
Founded 1967
Click to learn more

Perhaps the most powerful antiwar voices weren't the college students. They were the men who had actually been there. The VVAW organized veterans to march and speak out against the war they had fought. In 1971, hundreds of veterans marched on Washington and threw their medals onto the Capitol steps. One of them, a young Navy veteran named John Kerry, asked the Senate: "How do you ask a man to be the last man to die for a mistake?"

Students for a Democratic Society
SDS – Founded 1960
Click to learn more

The largest radical student organization in US history. SDS started by fighting racism and poverty, then turned its energy to Vietnam. Mostly white, middle-class college students, they organized sit-ins, teach-ins, and marches on campuses across the country. By 1969 they had over 100,000 members. The organization eventually fractured over increasingly radical tactics, but at its peak it was the engine of student opposition to the war.

The Yippies
Youth International Party, 1967
Click to learn more

If SDS was the serious wing of the movement, the Yippies were the circus. Founded by Abbie Hoffman and Jerry Rubin, they used absurdist theater to mock the war and the political establishment. They nominated a pig named Pigasus for president. They announced they would levitate the Pentagon. At the 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, their antics helped trigger a police riot broadcast live on national television, turning millions of viewers against the war.

Chapter 5
Why Did the US Fail in Vietnam?
Failed Objectives and Misunderstanding the Enemy

The United States never lost a major battle in Vietnam. Think about that. By almost every conventional military measure, America dominated. And still it lost the war. How?

Start with the South Vietnamese government. The US was fighting to defend a government that its own people didn't trust or believe in. A parade of military coups replaced one corrupt leader with another. The ARVN, South Vietnam's army, was plagued by low morale, poor leadership, and soldiers who had been forced into service for a cause they didn't feel was theirs. You can't win a war for a people who won't fight for themselves.

Then there was the fundamental misreading of the enemy. American commanders measured progress in body counts and kill ratios, assuming that if they killed enough North Vietnamese soldiers, the North would eventually quit. But Ho Chi Minh had told his people from the beginning: we will lose ten men for every one of yours, and we will still win. He meant it. North Vietnam absorbed casualties that would have broken any Western army and kept fighting.

The Ho Chi Minh Trail was another failure. The US dropped more bombs on Southeast Asia than it dropped in all of World War II. The Trail kept moving. North Vietnam could absorb almost any military punishment and keep going, because time was on their side.

Nixon's answer was Vietnamization, gradually transferring combat responsibility to the ARVN so US troops could come home. The Paris Peace Accords were signed in January 1973. American prisoners of war came home. US combat forces left. And the North Vietnamese waited exactly two years before finishing what they started.

By the time Nixon took office in 1969, the question wasn't whether to leave. It was how to leave without it looking like what it was: a defeat.
Richard Nixon
US President, 1969–1974
Click to learn more
He ran on a "secret plan" to end the war. There was no plan. Nixon secretly expanded the bombing into Cambodia and Laos while publicly claiming he was winding the war down. He achieved a negotiated exit, but South Vietnam fell two years after American forces left. Nixon resigned in 1974 over Watergate, a scandal that grew directly out of tactics his administration used against antiwar activists. Vietnam and Watergate together broke something in American public life that took a generation to rebuild.
Henry Kissinger
National Security Advisor
Click to learn more
Nixon's foreign policy architect and the man who negotiated the Paris Peace Accords. Kissinger won the Nobel Peace Prize for it, one of the most controversial awards in the prize's history. His critics pointed out he had helped extend the war by four years through secret bombing campaigns, and that the peace he negotiated was one South Vietnam couldn't survive. The North Vietnamese negotiator declined to accept his half of the prize.
Chapter 6
What Is the Legacy of Vietnam?
The Long Shadow of Defeat
The fall of Saigon, April 29, 1975

On April 30, 1975, North Vietnamese tanks rolled into Saigon. The last Americans scrambled onto helicopter rooftops. South Vietnam ceased to exist. It had taken exactly two years after the US withdrawal for the war to end the way the North always said it would.

The numbers were staggering. 58,300 Americans killed. Hundreds of thousands more wounded, many carrying invisible wounds that the country was barely equipped to understand. Approximately 2 million Vietnamese civilians dead. Three times the bomb tonnage of World War II dropped on Southeast Asia. One trillion dollars spent on a war that ultimately failed.

But the deepest costs weren't measured in dollars or casualties. Vietnam shattered the public's trust in government in ways that have never fully healed. The lies of the Johnson years, exposed by the Pentagon Papers. The deceptions of Nixon, confirmed by Watergate. A generation of Americans learned that their leaders would look them in the eye and lie about a war that was killing their sons.

Congress responded with the War Powers Act of 1973, requiring the president to consult Congress before committing troops to combat. A direct attempt to make sure no future president could slide into another Vietnam, one small commitment at a time, with no real debate.

The Vietnam Syndrome shaped American foreign policy for a generation. When Reagan wanted to send troops to Central America, opponents called it "another Vietnam." When the US invaded Iraq in 2003, critics warned from the start about the parallels. Vietnam became the measuring stick for every military commitment that followed.

And the soldiers who came home? They returned to a country that often didn't know how to receive them, not celebrated like WWII veterans, sometimes actively resented. It took years for American culture to begin to reckon honestly with what those men and women had been asked to do, and what had been done to them.

58,000 Americans. Millions of Vietnamese. A trillion dollars. A generation that lost its faith in its government. The Vietnam War didn't just end. It left a mark on American politics, American culture, and the American military that you can still trace today, if you know where to look.
